write.desc: This topic studies series of the form sum a_n (x - c)^n: where they converge, why convergence is uniform only on smaller closed intervals, how they can be differentiated and integrated term by term, and when a smooth function actually equals its Taylor series. The points belong together because each one builds on the radius of convergence and on applying the interchange theorems to this one well-behaved family of series.

points.name: Power series and the shape of their convergence set
points.what: Recognise a power series sum a_n (x - c)^n with its centre and coefficients, and prove that if it converges at x0 then it converges absolutely at every x with |x - c| < |x0 - c|, by comparison with a geometric series. This shows the set where it converges is an interval centred at c (possibly a single point or all of R).
outside: comparison test for series of nonnegative terms
terms of a convergent series tend to zero

points.name: Radius of convergence: the Cauchy-Hadamard formula
points.what: Define the radius of convergence R and prove R = 1 / limsup |a_n|^(1/n) (with the conventions 1/0 = infinity and 1/infinity = 0) using the root test: the series converges absolutely for |x - c| < R and diverges for |x - c| > R. Compute R with justification for series whose coefficients have no simple ratio.

points.name: The ratio form of the radius and its limits
points.what: Use R = lim |a_n / a_(n+1)| when that limit exists, justified by the ratio test, as the quick way to find the radius in most examples. Recognise when it fails, such as series with gaps like sum x^(2n) / 4^n or oscillating coefficients, and fall back on Cauchy-Hadamard.

points.name: Behaviour at the endpoints
points.what: Understand that the radius says nothing about the points x = c +- R, which must be tested separately with series tests. Know the standard examples sum x^n (diverges at both ends), sum x^n / n (converges at -1 only) and sum x^n / n^2 (converges at both), and find the exact interval of convergence of a given series.
outside: divergence when terms do not tend to zero

points.name: Uniform convergence on closed subintervals and continuity of the sum
points.what: Prove with the Weierstrass M-test that a power series converges uniformly on every closed interval [c - r, c + r] with r < R, and conclude that its sum is continuous on the whole open interval of convergence. Show by the example sum x^n on (-1, 1) that convergence need not be uniform on the full open interval.
outside: uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (series form)

points.name: Term-by-term differentiation
points.what: Prove that the differentiated series sum n a_n (x - c)^(n-1) has the same radius of convergence (using lim n^(1/n) = 1 in Cauchy-Hadamard), and apply the term-by-term differentiation theorem on closed subintervals to show the sum f is differentiable with f' given by that series everywhere inside the interval. Conclude that f is infinitely differentiable there.
outside: theorem on differentiating a series of functions term by term under uniform convergence of the derivatives

points.name: Term-by-term integration and new series from old
points.what: Show that a power series can be integrated term by term on any interval inside its interval of convergence, giving a series with the same radius. Use this with substitution and differentiation to derive series such as log(1 + x) = sum (-1)^(n+1) x^n / n and arctan x = sum (-1)^n x^(2n+1) / (2n+1) from the geometric series.
outside: uniform convergence lets a limit pass through the Riemann integral

points.name: Abel's theorem at the endpoints
points.what: Know the statement of Abel's theorem: if a power series converges at an endpoint, its sum is continuous there from inside the interval (and convergence is uniform up to that endpoint). Use it to justify sums like log 2 = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ... and pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ..., and explain why continuity at the endpoint does not follow from the earlier results alone.

points.name: Coefficients are derivatives: uniqueness of power series
points.what: Prove by repeated term-by-term differentiation that if f(x) = sum a_n (x - c)^n near c then a_n = f^(n)(c) / n!. Conclude that a function has at most one power series expansion about a given centre, and use this to identify coefficients or compute high derivatives at c.

points.name: Taylor series and proving a function equals its series
points.what: Define the Taylor series of an infinitely differentiable function at c and understand that it converging is not the same as it converging to f. Prove f equals its Taylor series on an interval by showing the Taylor remainder tends to zero, as for e^x, sin x and cos x on all of R (using M^n / n! -> 0) and for log(1 + x) on (-1, 1].
outside: limit of M^n / n! is zero

points.name: Smooth but not analytic: e^(-1/x^2)
points.what: Prove that f(x) = e^(-1/x^2) for x != 0, f(0) = 0, is infinitely differentiable with every derivative zero at 0, so its Taylor series at 0 is identically zero yet f is not. Use it to state the difference between infinitely differentiable and analytic functions precisely.
outside: derivative as a limit of difference quotients
exponential decay beats any power: limits like e^(-1/x^2) / x^k -> 0

points.name: Weierstrass approximation theorem (stated)
points.what: Know the statement that every continuous function on [a, b] is a uniform limit of polynomials, and contrast it with Taylor series: the approximating polynomials are not partial sums of one series and exist even for functions like |x| or nowhere-differentiable functions that have no Taylor series at all.

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd edition)
where.detail: Sections 6.5 (Power Series), 6.6 (Taylor Series) and 6.7 (The Weierstrass Approximation Theorem)

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd edition)
where.detail: Chapter 8, Some Special Functions: power series, Abel's theorem and Taylor expansions; Theorem 7.26 for the Weierstrass approximation theorem

where.title: Michael Spivak, Calculus
where.detail: Chapter on uniform convergence and power series; chapter on approximation by polynomial functions for Taylor remainders

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Section 9.4 (Series of Functions), including power series; Section 6.4 (Taylor's Theorem)
